newsitem.title: UK: Demographic timebomb prompts UK pension shake-up.
newsitem.headline: Demographic timebomb prompts UK pension shake-up.

text.p: Pension provision in Britain is facing one its biggest ever shake-ups following announcement by the Labour government on Thursday of a wide-ranging pensions review.
At the top of the agenda is a government aim that in the future everyone has access to a second pension to supplement the basic state pension.

The review is an attempt to head off the demographic problems of an ageing population, which are faced by all developed economies, and to answer difficult questions about how pensions should be paid for.
The costs involved have already led the government to ditch a commitment of the 1980s to restore a link between pension rises and earnings.
The need for reform of the present system are clear.

A recent report by the Office of Fair Trading found that around 25 percent of the workforce have no pension provision and some 45 percent of the adult population will rely on the state for income unless adequate provision is made.
Among non-pensioners, one third of men and more than half of women have no pension arrangements.
Pension payments comprise far and away the biggest single component of the welfare budget.
The basic state pension is expected to cost 31.9 billion pounds ($53.5 billion) this year, roughly one third of the total social security budget of 96.7 billion pounds.
And the problems of paying pensions to a rising proportion of the population are set to increase.
In Britain the number of the population aged 65 and over is expected to increase from 16 percent in 1990 to 23 percent by 2030.
The contribution ratio of those in the active labour force to those in receipt of pensions is projected to fall from 2.1 in 2000 to 1.6 by 2030 according to the government actuary.
Thursday's review was promised by Labour last year at its party conference in Blackpool.

The thinking behind a second tier 'stakeholder pension' is to provide a top up to the basic pension which would be an alternative to state-earnings related pensions (Serps) and would be aimed at the millions of people in work who are unable to join an occupational scheme run by an employer.
The government is also looking at the introduction of 'citizenship pensions' aimed at those for example caring for elderly relatives and unable to to contribute to pensions in their own right.
Both proposals are to be implemented in the current Parliament, set to last for up to five years from the government's election in May.

The government has been under pressure from the opposition Conservatives and pensions industry since Chancellor Gordon Brown's recent budget removed the main tax concession available to pension funds, a move which the Conservatives dubbed a "five billion pound smash and grab raid" on pensions.

In the run up to the last election the Conservatives put forward their own solution to the pensions issue, called Basic Pensions Plus, which involved a gradual switch to people building up their own pension funds over their working life.
The crisis in pension provision in Britain was highlighted earlier this week by a damning OFT report on the shortcomings of existing pension products.
It called for radical changes to safeguard consumer interests and for the government to incorporate a new, flexible pension product.
The OFT criticised personal pension plans for providing poor value with benefits frequently being eroded by the high cost of marketing and fund management.
While it said that occupational pensions might have improved in recent years, those who left early -- as the majority do -- lost out.
Employees who moved employers several times could find their occupational pension up to 30 percent lower than someone who stayed in the same scheme.
Alongside existing providers, the OFT envisaged alternative channels for the new pension product, such as building societies or unions.
